Choosing the best electric motorcycle gear starts with one insight that petrol riders rarely think about: there is no engine heat. On a bike like the Zero DSR/X there is no warm cylinder radiating up at your knees, no exhaust taking the edge off a cold morning, and crucially no heat to help evaporate the rain off your gear. Everything that keeps you warm has to come from what you wear, which changes the priorities completely. After a full winter riding electric around the north of England, I am convinced that weather protection and heated kit matter more on an EV than on almost anything else.

Why electric gear priorities are different

On a combustion tourer such as a BMW R 1250 GS, the engine and exhaust throw off enough warmth to take the sting out of a cold ride and even help dry damp gloves. Ride an EV and all of that disappears. You also often ride at a smooth, quiet, steady pace that means you are exposed to cold air for longer without the fidgety warmth of a revving engine beneath you. The upside is a wonderfully refined ride; the downside is that you feel the cold and the wet sooner, so your kit has to do all the work.

Heated kit is not a luxury, it is the point

This is where electric riders should lean in. Modern heated gear is superb, and an electric bike has plenty of accessory power to run it. A pair of Keis G701 Heated Gloves keeps your hands working on a frozen run over the A82 at Glencoe, and a Keis V501 Heated Vest heats your core so the rest of you stops shivering. Add a set of Oxford Heaterz Premium Heated Grips and you have a warm cockpit that a petrol bike can only dream of. Our heated motorcycle gloves guide compares battery versus hard-wired options, and on an EV I lean towards wiring into the bike where possible.

On my first winter EV ride I dressed like I would on my old petrol tourer and froze within twenty minutes. There was simply no engine warmth to fall back on. Heated kit turned it from an ordeal into a pleasure.

Weatherproofing matters more without engine heat

Because nothing on the bike helps dry you out, staying dry in the first place is essential. A quality laminated jacket like a Halvarssons Laminated Touring Jacket keeps the wet out for hours rather than minutes, which is exactly what you want when there is no warmth to help. Our waterproof motorcycle jackets guide explains why laminated construction beats a drop-liner for sustained rain, and on an EV that difference is amplified.

Carry a proper oversuit

Even with a good jacket, I keep a packable Oxford Rainseal Oversuit aboard. It weighs almost nothing, seals up your legs, and gives you a dry outer shell for the worst of a Bealach na Ba squall. On a combustion bike you might risk riding through a shower to dry off later; on an EV there is no drying off, so you suit up early.

Quiet helmets suit a quiet bike

One of the joys of electric riding is the near silence, and it feels a shame to spoil it with wind roar. A refined, low-noise helmet lets you appreciate the calm. A Schuberth C5 Helmet is one of the quietest touring lids you can buy, with an excellent seal and an integrated comms antenna, so you can enjoy music or navigation prompts over almost no background noise. On an EV, where wind is the only real sound, a quiet helmet transforms the experience.

Lightweight layering for efficiency

Range anxiety is real on an electric bike, and heavy, bulky gear that makes you work harder does you no favours. I favour a system of thin, warm layers rather than one huge coat. A sensible layering plan looks like this:

  • A merino base layer for warmth without bulk.
  • A heated vest as the mid layer, drawing on the bike or its own battery.
  • A laminated waterproof jacket as the outer shell.
  • Heated gloves rather than enormous winter gauntlets that spoil throttle feel.
  • A slim neck tube to seal the gap at your collar.

Range, planning and comfort

Because your gear is doing the heating, it also protects your range by keeping you comfortable enough to ride efficiently rather than tensing against the cold. Plan charging stops to double as warm-up breaks, and you will find electric touring genuinely relaxing. Our full guide to electric motorcycle touring in the UK covers charging strategy in detail, which pairs neatly with getting your kit right.

The verdict

The best electric motorcycle gear in the UK is built around a simple truth: your bike will not keep you warm or dry, so your kit has to. Prioritise heated gloves, a heated vest and heated grips, wrap it in a laminated waterproof outer, carry an oversuit, and choose a quiet helmet to savour the silence. Get that combination right and an EV becomes the most comfortable, refined way to ride through a British winter, no engine heat required.

Heated gloves, a heated vest and heated grips are the point, not a luxury, on an EV.
Weatherproofing matters more without engine warmth to dry you out; laminated jackets keep the wet out for hours.
A quiet, refined helmet lets you enjoy the near-silence of electric riding.
Lightweight thin layers protect range better than heavy, bulky gear.
